items.title: Galectin-3 links microglial neuroinflammation to Aβ aggregation and lysosomal processing.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
items.authors: Lluís Camprubí-Ferrer; Jesús Soldán-Hidalgo; Emil Axell; Marzia Dell'Eva; Marta García-Cruzado; Juan García-Revilla; Yiyi Yang; Rosalía Fernández-Calle
items.abstract: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the molecular mechanisms linking microglial dysfunction to amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify galectin-3 (Gal3) as a regulator of plaque-associated microglial responses, linking Aβ aggregation, lysosomal function, and neuritic pathology. Using postmortem brain tissue from AD patients, we found that Gal3+ microglia preferentially associate with cored plaques and correlate with increased LAMP1+ dystrophic neurites. Gal3 was also detected in microglial lysosomal compartments, extramicroglial dystrophic structures, and in association with extracellular amyloid fibrils, suggesting roles in both intracellular and extracellular Aβ processing. In APP mice, Gal3 deficiency reduced plaque burden and neuritic dystrophy, increased plaque compaction, and enhanced TREM2 coverage around amyloid plaques. Mechanistically, in vitro microglial experiments showed that Gal3 modulates Aβ uptake and lysosomal processing, whereas lysosomal dysfunction promoted the accumulation of fibrillar Aβ from initially monomeric species, particularly in Gal3-deficient cells. Cell-free assays demonstrated that Gal3 preferentially binds fibrillar Aβ, inhibits secondary nucleation, and alters fibril morphology, while Gal3-modified fibrillar Aβ reduces N2a neuronal cell number. Finally, in silico structural analyses identified candidate Gal3 interactors enriched in leucine-rich-repeat and immunoglobulin-like proteins, supporting a role for this lectin in immune receptor regulation. Complementary in vivo transcriptomic profiling showed that Gal3 deletion suppresses type I interferon and microglial neurodegenerative transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings position Gal3 at the interface between Aβ remodeling, lysosomal homeostasis, and plaque-associated microglial responses in AD.

items.title: Intranasal delivery of a ROS-activatable myeloperoxidase inhibitor alleviates Alzheimer's-like symptoms and pathology.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
items.authors: Jing Wang; Peilin Cong; Enduo Feng; Matthias W G Zeller; Boyu Zhang; Yifan Lv; Negin Jalali Motlagh; Jenny Linnoila
items.abstract: Chronic neuroinflammation and oxidative stress are important contributors to Alzheimer's disease (AD). Myeloperoxidase (MPO), a key driver of oxidative inflammation released mainly by activated microglia in the neurodegenerative brain, is a potential therapeutic target to inhibit the neuroinflammatory cascade and oxidative damage in AD, but the underlying mechanisms remain unexplored, and achieving targeted brain delivery of an MPO inhibitor and minimizing systemic effects remain significant challenges. We addressed these limitations by first establishing that genetic deletion of MPO in the 5XFAD mouse model improved memory performance and reduced amyloid deposition, validating MPO as a therapeutic target. We then developed a liposome-encapsulated reactive oxygen species (ROS)-activatable MPO inhibitor (LERAMI). LERAMI uniquely combines targeted delivery with on-demand drug release, utilizing a ROS-sensitive linker to selectively release MPO inhibitors in ROS-rich regions within the AD microenvironment, minimizing off-target effects and systemic toxicity. In the 5XFAD mouse model. By reducing MPO expression and activity, LERAMI significantly improved cognitive performance, accompanied by decreased microglial activation, attenuated oxidative DNA damage, improved synaptic and neuronal density, and reduced amyloid burden. RNA sequencing revealed a robust hippocampal transcriptomic reprogramming, with upregulation of pathways critical for synaptic plasticity, calcium signaling, axon guidance, and neuroprotection, along with downregulation of inflammatory and immune response pathways. These findings demonstrate that targeted ROS-activatable MPO inhibition with LERAMI represents a promising therapeutic strategy for AD and potentially other neuroinflammatory diseases, offering a unique approach to mitigate neuroinflammation, preserve synaptic integrity, and restore cognitive function.

items.title: A study on olfactory mucosa-derived stem cells for ischemic stroke is registered in Hainan.
items.abstract: On November 4, 2026, China announced that a study on autologous olfactory mucosa-derived mesenchymal stem cells for ischemic stroke was registered in Hainan. Initiated by Hainan Susheng Biotechnology Co., Ltd., the project lists Haikou People's Hospital as its clinical research institution. Olfactory mucosa-derived cells provide a distinct source for investigating immunomodulation and neural repair. A 2025 study of hypoxia-preconditioned cells reported reduced microglial ferroptosis and neuroinflammation and improved neurological outcomes in experimental stroke models. These findings provide a preclinical rationale; the registered product's preparation and its effects in humans need to be clinically evaluated. For Hainan, the project links local scientific work with collaboration between a biotechnology enterprise and a hospital. Its contribution will depend on appropriate patient selection, credible study design, meaningful functional outcomes, reproducible cell manufacture, and long-term safety monitoring. Transparent reporting can make this experience informative for future stroke research and the development of regulated regenerative medicine.

items.title: Integrated QTL mapping and CRISPR screening in pooled iPSC-derived microglia reveals genetic drivers of neurodegenerative risk.
items.authors: Marta Perez-Alcantara; Sam J Washer; Yixi Chen; Juliette Steer; Daianna Gonzalez-Padilla; Joe McWilliam; David Willé; Nikolaos Panousis
items.abstract: Mounting evidence implicates microglia in neurodegeneration, but linking disease-associated genetic variants to target genes and cellular phenotypes is hindered by the inaccessibility of these cells. We differentiated 261 human induced pluripotent stem cell lines into microglia-like (iMGL) cells in pools with phenotypic (differentiation, phagocytosis and migration) and single-cell transcriptomic readouts. Burden analysis of deleterious variants detected 36 genes influencing microglial phenotypes. Expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) analysis identified 7,121 eQTL-associated genes and 79 colocalizations across four neurodegenerative disease genome-wide association studies, half of which had limited prior evidence of causality. Integration of eQTL and phenotypic associations highlighted the role of disease-relevant variants, including LRRK2 and TREM2 acting through microglial phagocytosis. A coupled CRISPR screen identified a role for TREM2 in phagocytosis and highlighted the importance of cell type in the directionality of phenotypic effects. By contextualizing variant effects within iMGLs in different inflammatory states, we provide a comprehensive framework for interpreting the function of risk loci in neurodegenerative disorders.

items.title: Neuronal IL-34 programs microglial activity via the TGF-β-MEF2C axis to constrain neuroinflammation following brain ischemia.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
items.authors: Minshu Li; Xu Zhou; Ran Li; Hanchen Liu; Caiyun Qi; Wenjun Zhang; Yali Han; Tingyu Yin
items.abstract: Brain ischemia induces robust neuroinflammation driven by microglial activation, yet whether ischemic neurons actively reprogram microglial phenotypes to limit inflammation remains elusive. Here, we identify neuronal interleukin-34 (IL-34) as a critical immunomodulatory signal that maintains microglial homeostasis after cerebral ischemia. We demonstrate that ischemic injury augments IL-34-CSF1R signaling between neurons and microglia. Neuron-specific overexpression of Il34 (Syn1-Il34tg mice) attenuated infarct volume and neurodeficits after middle cerebral artery occlusion, whereas neuronal Il34 knockdown exacerbated brain injury. Microglial depletion abolished IL-34-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting microglia as essential effectors. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that neuronal IL-34 preserved homeostatic microglial signatures (P2ry12, Cx3cr1, Tgfbr1), while suppressing inflammatory activities (Il1b, Tnf, Cxcl2) through upregulation of the transcription factor MEF2C. Mechanistically, IL-34 activated TGF-β signaling in microglia and inhibition of TGF-β signaling abolished the protective effects of IL-34, whereas microglia-specific Mef2c overexpression rescued neuroprotection despite TGF-β blockade. Thus, ischemic neurons deploy IL-34 to orchestrate the immunoregulatory activity of microglia via the TGF-β-MEF2C axis, representing a previously unrecognized endogenous mechanism counteracting neuroinflammation. Our study reveals neuronal IL-34 as a potential therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

We demonstrate that ischemic injury augments IL-34-CSF1R signaling between neurons and microglia. Neuron-specific overexpression of Il34 (Syn1-Il34tg mice) attenuated infarct volume and neurodeficits after middle cerebral artery occlusion, whereas neuronal Il34 knockdown exacerbated brain injury. Microglial depletion abolished IL-34-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting microglia as essential effectors. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that neuronal IL-34 preserved homeostatic microglial signatures (P2ry12, Cx3cr1, Tgfbr1), while suppressing inflammatory activities (Il1b, Tnf, Cxcl2) through upregulation of the transcription factor MEF2C. Mechanistically, IL-34 activated TGF-β signaling in microglia and inhibition of TGF-β signaling abolished the protective effects of IL-34, whereas microglia-specific Mef2c overexpression rescued neuroprotection despite TGF-β blockade. Thus, ischemic neurons deploy IL-34 to orchestrate the immunoregulatory activity of microglia via the TGF-β-MEF2C axis, representing a previously unrecognized endogenous mechanism counteracting neuroinflammation. Our study reveals neuronal IL-34 as a potential therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

items.title: Pluripotent stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles for systemic immune modulation in diabetes therapy.
items.authors: Jana Zarubova; Mohammad Mahdi Hasani-Sadrabadi; Yutong Wu; Graciel Diamante; Jenny Cheng; Soomin Park; Xiao Han; Fatemeh Sadat Majedi
items.abstract: Embryonic development is characterized by remarkable immune tolerance, yet whether this property extends to pluripotent stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) has remained unclear. Here we show that EVs from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs), including embryonic stem cells and induced pluripotent stem cells, outperform mesenchymal stem cell-derived EVs in suppressing proinflammatory cytokine secretion, reducing T cell activation and inducing regulatory T cells. PSC EVs display distinct molecular signatures, containing unique proteins and microRNAs absent from mesenchymal stem cell-derived EVs, including the pluripotency-associated proteins ROR1 and CD133 and members of the miR-302 family. Dynamic suspension culture of PSC aggregates enhances the EV yield, providing a scalable and reproducible source. Delivered via a biomaterial scaffold, two local injections of induced PSC EVs significantly improved diabetes-free survival in an antigen-specific type 1 diabetes model, increasing regulatory T cell populations in draining lymph nodes, as well as inducing systemic immune modulation and preserving β-cell mass. These findings establish PSC EVs as a scalable immunomodulatory platform for autoimmune disease and for immune tolerance in cell therapy.

items.title: miR-665 ameliorates neuroinflammation after intracerebral hemorrhage by modulating myeloid cell polarization via targeting STAT3.
items.authors: Zhangliang Huang; Yuqi Yang; Bing Sun; Jianing Luo; Yongxiang Yang; Dongbo Zou; Yongquan Cui; Lekai Wang
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Microglia-mediated neuroinflammation contributes to secondary injury after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), but the role of miR-665 remains unclear. METHODS: An ICH rat model was established. A combination of techniques, including Neurological scoring, brain water content measurement, histology and molecular assays were employed to assess miR-665, the STAT3/NF-κB pathway, myeloid polarization and inflammation. Stereotaxic miR-665 agomir/antagomir delivery verified its function. The targeting relationship between miR-665 and STAT3 was confirmed by a dual-luciferase reporter assay. In vitro experiments were performed in Hemin-stimulated BV2 cells with miR-665 mimics/inhibitor, followed by flow cytometry detection of cell polarization and inflammatory factor analysis. Rescue experiments with STAT3 overexpression were conducted both in vivo and in vitro. RESULTS: After ICH, miR-665 was downregulated andinduced excessive activation of the STAT3/NF-κB signaling axis in peri-hematomal tissue, accompanied by M1-like/pro-inflammatory myeloid cell polarization and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines. Upregulation of miR-665 ameliorated neurological function, reduced brain edema, promoted M2-like/repair-associated polarization, and suppressed inflammation, whereas miR-665 downregulation aggravated injury. Dual-luciferase assay confirmed that miR-665 directly targets STAT3. In vitro, miR-665 overexpression inhibited STAT3 phosphorylation and further suppressed the downstream NF-κB signaling, reversing the Hemin-induced M1-like/pro-inflammatory polarization. STAT3 overexpression counteracted the protective effects of miR-665. CONCLUSION: Downregulated miR-665 after ICH exacerbates neuroinflammation by promoting M1-like/pro-inflammatory myeloid cell polarization via disinhibition of STAT3 and subsequent activation of NF-κB signaling. Upregulating miR-665 exerts neuroprotection by inhibiting STAT3 phosphorylation and facilitating M2-like/repair-associated myeloid cell polarization, highlighting the miR-665/STAT3 regulatory cascade as a promising therapeutic target for post-ICH neuroinflammation.

items.title: CaSiO
items.authors: Jiewen Liao; Lizhi Ouyang; Ruiyin Zeng; Al-Smadi Fawwaz; Qipeng Wu; Xi He; Yun Sun; Hang Xue
items.abstract: Diabetes impairs fracture healing. In diabetic mice, we found that PGC-1α expression is downregulated in bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC). PGC-1α levels positively correlate with osteogenic capacity. Physiologically, reduced PGC-1α suppresses miR-363-3p expression; mechanistically, this further inhibits DKK3, thereby promoting β-catenin phosphorylation and degradation, which in turn inhibits osteogenesis in BMSCs. To target this pathway, we treated BMSC with calcium silicate (CaSiO3). CaSiO3 inhibited the ubiquitination-mediated degradation of PGC-1α, restoring miR-363-3p expression. It also upregulated AGO2, which facilitated the assembly of miR-363-3p into mi-RISC complexes and their loading into extracellular vesicles. We then engineered a ROS-responsive hydrogel (GelROS) to deliver these CaSiO3-engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs). In diabetic mice with femoral fractures, the hydrogel enabled sustained, on-demand release of EVs specifically at sites with high ROS levels. The released EVs, enriched with miRISC complexes, suppressed the DKK3-β-catenin axis in recipient BMSC, enhanced osteogenesis, and accelerated fracture healing. This study identifies the PGC-1α-miR-363-3p-DKK3-β-catenin axis as a key pathway in diabetic fracture healing. It also presents a novel EVs-based strategy that avoids direct CaSiO3 toxicity, offering a new translational approach for treating diabetic bone defects.

items.title: Fast-scan cyclic voltammetry for real-time serotonin dynamics in human iPSC-derived neural spheroids.
items.authors: Bettina Bohl; Pablo Prieto; Tomas Andriuškevičius; Joanna Mialkowska; Tom Burton; Matthew Murphy; Charlie Rayner; James W Hardin
items.abstract: Measuring neurotransmission in the human brain could advance our understanding of disorders, including depression. Although fast-scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) has provided valuable insights into neurotransmission in animal models, its application to human systems remains challenging. Here, we present an FSCV-based framework for real-time serotonin measurements in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived three-dimensional (3D) neuronal cultures. We demonstrate reproducible detection of spontaneous and evoked serotonin release from 3D serotonergic spheroids and show that serotonin dynamics differ between serotonin reuptake inhibitors. We investigate how a molecular stress mediator influences serotonin signaling and antidepressant effectiveness. Finally, we extend the platform to co-cultures containing microglia-like cells to examine serotonin dynamics under inflammatory conditions. We present a translational, label-free technology to measure serotonin dynamics in real-time in human stem cell-derived models. This method studies serotonin regulation, with potential applications to drug development and the mechanistic dissection of psychiatric disorders, such as depression.

items.title: Spheroid-laden hydrogels with dual biomimetic intra- and perispheroidal niches for enhanced bone healing.
items.authors: Yujin Han; Hyunseok Kwon; Woo Hyuk Jung; Seung Jae Huh; Goen Lee; Dong June Ahn; Heungsoo Shin
items.abstract: Stem cell spheroid-hydrogel platforms offer promise for bone defect repair, but implantation-associated oxidative stress, poor vascular ingrowth, and insufficient osteogenic cues limit their clinical translation. Here, we developed dual-NICHE (dual niche-instructive construct for bone healing and engraftment), a gelatin methacryloyl hydrogel containing human adipose-derived stem cell spheroids with spatially distinct intra-/perispheroidal niches. Within a single construct, these two niches provide complementary functions to simultaneously address the key bottlenecks in bone regeneration. The intraspheroidal niche incorporated bone morphogenetic protein-2-immobilized fibers to promote osteogenic differentiation, whereas the perispheroidal matrix contained Sr2+-tannic acid nanoparticles (NPs). Upon implantation, the NPs mitigated oxidative stress and supported vascular infiltration. Concurrently, the osteogenic cue promoted differentiation, while the NPs facilitated mineral nucleation and growth, as further supported by molecular dynamics simulations. Together, this spatial integration enhanced vascularized bone formation with a bone volume fraction of ∼13.5% using only 5208 cells per defect in a mouse calvarial model, providing a potentially translatable framework for bone regeneration.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Agent Orange Exposure and Diagnosis of Parkinson Disease and Related Disorders Among US Veterans.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Gregory D Scott; Miranda M Lim; Jonathan E Elliott; Lee E Neilson
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: IMPORTANCE: The risk of Parkinson disease (PD) due to Agent Orange, the Vietnam War Era defoliant, is inferred from studies of agricultural pesticide exposure. Epidemiological work is currently lacking. OBJECTIVE: To examine the association between Agent Orange exposure with incident cases of synucleinopathies including Parkinson disease, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) among US veterans. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This was an electronic health record-based cohort study inclusive of medical records from January 1, 1999, to December 30, 2022. Veterans were followed up for a mean (SD) of 12.5 (7.0) years from the start of records. Analyses were conducted from July 2024 to July 2026. The setting was the US Department of Veterans Affairs and included US veterans who served during the Vietnam War Era (August 1964 to May 1975) were screened. Those with incomplete demographic data or prevalent synucleinopathies before or within 6 months of follow-up were excluded. EXPOSURE: Agent Orange defined by self-report. Direct or occupational exposure was defined by involvement in Operation Ranch Hand, Army Chemical Corps, and/or direct handling or spraying. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Cumulative incidence of synucleinopathies was calculated adjusting for competing risk of death, age, traumatic brain injury, and frailty. RESULTS: After screening of 4 917 272 US veterans, 4 468 509 veterans (mean [SD] age, 60.6 [8] years; 4 380 139 male [98%]) were included in analyses. A total of 1 035 210 veterans (23.2%) had Agent Orange exposure; 7600 (0.2%) of these had direct or occupational exposure. Birth year, age at time 0 (start of records), sex, race, ethnicity, and smoking history were balanced among the exposed and unexposed groups with further adjustment for traumatic brain injury and frailty. Agent Orange exposure was associated with higher risk of PD (hazard ratio [HR], 1.44; 95% CI, 1.37-1.52), RBD (HR, 1.78; 95% CI, 1.68-1.89), and DLB (HR, 1.66; 95% CI, 1.32-2.09). Associations strengthened when enriched for direct or occupational exposure, including PD (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.71-2.32) and RBD (HR, 2.25; 95% CI, 1.87-2.70). Results were robust to additional adjustment for traumatic brain injury, frailty, health care utilization, and multiple imputation. Sensitivity analyses indicated that substantial unmeasured confounding would be required to explain the observed associations. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Results of this cohort study suggest that Agent Orange may be an independent risk factor for later development of PD and related conditions. This finding has implications for global policy change. Further studies are needed to understand the mechanism underlying this association, gene-toxin interactions, and whether there is a unique clinical phenotype to those exposed to Agent Orange.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Hypersensitivity to adrenomedullin in post-traumatic headache: a randomized crossover study.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Haidar M Al-Khazali; Zahra Hakimzadeh; Anna G Melchior; Berkay Alpay; Ksenija Cucanić; Annette M Fuchs; Messoud Ashina; Håkan Ashina
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Adrenomedullin (ADM), a vasoactive member of the calcitonin peptide family with receptor-signalling overlap with calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), has emerged as a candidate therapeutic target in migraine. Given the striking clinical parallels between migraine and persistent post-traumatic headache (PTH), we investigated whether ADM-responsive signalling contributes to migraine-like headache in adults with persistent PTH attributed to mild traumatic brain injury. We conducted a single-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-way crossover study in adults with persistent PTH and no pre-trauma history of migraine. On two experimental days separated by at least 7 days, participants received 20-minute intravenous infusions of ADM (19.9 pmol kg⁻¹ min⁻¹) and isotonic saline as the matched inactive comparator (placebo) in randomised sequence. Headache outcomes were recorded for 12 hours. The primary outcome was the within-participant incidence of experimentally induced migraine-like headache. The secondary outcome was the within-participant difference in baseline-corrected area under the curve (AUC) for headache intensity from 0 to 12 hours. Of 158 individuals assessed for eligibility, 21 were randomised, completed both periods and were analysed. Participants had a mean age of 34.3 years, 19 (90%) were female, and 18 (86%) reported a migraine-like phenotype. Migraine-like headache occurred in 17 of 21 participants (81%) after ADM and four of 21 (19%) following placebo. Fourteen participants developed migraine-like only after ADM and one only following placebo, yielding a paired absolute risk difference of 61.9 percentage points (95% CI 29.7-80.6; one-sided P < 0.001; two-sided P = 0.001). Baseline-corrected headache-intensity AUC was higher after ADM than placebo (median 1,110 [IQR 315-2205] versus 420 [-160 to 565]; P = 0.006). Median time to onset of migraine-like headache was 30 minutes after ADM and 390 minutes following placebo. Fifteen participants reported that the ADM-induced headache resembled their usual migraine-like headache episodes, and rescue medication was used by 10 participants after ADM and two after placebo. These findings identify pronounced responsiveness to ADM-linked signalling in persistent PTH and support the ADM pathway as a candidate target for mechanism-based therapeutic development, pending confirmation in independent cohorts and complementary preclinical studies.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer's disease.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Doudou Yu; Jürgen Germann; Ghulam Murtaza; Kaitlyn H Hajdarovic; Kelsey R Babcock; Shiva Kazempour Dehkordi; Alexander C Jackson; Ivana Delalle
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand-receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Microglia mediate motor memory decay through activity-dependent phagocytosis of myelin sheaths.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Zhechun Hu; Yujian Luo; Tingqi Zhou; Xuan Wu; Jiao Ma; Chao Wang; Liang Wang; Xiao-Dong Wang
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Experience-dependent changes in myelination are important for motor learning, with newly generated oligodendrocytes contributing to the formation of new myelin. However, motor memories decay over time and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here we show that motor memory decay is linked to changes in memory-associated myelin sheaths resulting from microglial phagocytosis in mouse brain. Mechanistically, reduced activity of motor memory engram cells lowers oligodendrocyte expression of the 'don't eat me' signal from Cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47), facilitating microglial phagocytosis and driving myelin loss. Knockout of CD47 from motor memory-associated oligodendrocytes increased microglial phagocytosis of myelin sheaths and accelerated the decay of motor memory, whereas overexpression of CD47 showed opposite results. Moreover, microglia phagocytose myelin sheaths and synapses independently. Our findings reveal that microglial phagocytosis of motor memory-associated myelin sheaths leads to the decay of motor memory. Since various types of memory require myelination in the brain, this mechanism may contribute to the decay of other memory types.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: A cell-type-resolved proteomic atlas reveals intra- and intercellular signaling in Alzheimer's disease.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Xue Zhang; Jiyuan Yang; Kaiwen Yu; Him K Shrestha; Ying Zhou; Yun Jiao; Ju Wang; Ping-Chung Chen
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) arises from pathological interactions among diverse brain cell types, but cell-type-specific proteomic changes remain underexplored. Here, we present deep proteomic profiling of sorted or proximity-labeled brain cells from AD mouse models (5xFAD and AppNL-G-F) at multiple ages, quantifying 13,411 proteins in microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, and neurons, with additional spatial information. We identified 3,028 differentially abundant proteins, most of which were absent in a bulk proteomic dataset, and constructed cell-type-specific networks to define functional modules and hub proteins. Comparison with transcriptomic data revealed that ∼30% of proteomic changes are RNA discordant. Further analyses uncovered cross-cell-type signaling proteins conserved in human AD brains, such as pleiotrophin (Ptn), which is transcriptionally enriched in astrocytes but accumulates in microglia. Importantly, recombinant PTN activates human induced microglia (iMG) cells. Thus, these findings provide a comprehensive cell-type-resolved proteomic atlas of AD models, highlighting novel intra- and intercellular signaling events.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Sex-dependent spatial organization of microgliosis tracks synaptic pathology in the demyelinated superior colliculus.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Jackson David McGrath; John Shultz; Maia J Classe; D Ford Hannum; Sebastian Werneburg
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Visual impairment is a common and clinically salient manifestation of Multiple Sclerosis (MS), yet pathology across visual system structures remains incompletely defined. Although the optic nerve, lateral geniculate nucleus, and visual cortex have been extensively studied, involvement of the superior colliculus (SC), a key visual processing hub, remains unclear. Here, we combined human postmortem tissue analysis with functional assessment and spatial mapping in the MS-relevant cuprizone (CPZ) mouse model to define how demyelination and secondary injury are organized within the SC. Postmortem SC tissue from donors with MS revealed myelin loss, including focal demyelinated lesions. In mice, CPZ impaired visual function and induced widespread SC demyelination without detectable neuronal loss or axonal degeneration. In male mice, although diffuse demyelination was accompanied by widespread microgliosis, atlas-based mapping uncovered a previously unrecognized spatial organization: a discrete high-microgliosis compartment with a stereotyped location and shape in every CPZ-treated mouse. This compartment did not correspond to canonical SC maps and was not explained by baseline microglial or myelin differences or by variability in local demyelination severity. Instead, high-microgliosis regions showed increased synaptic elimination, suggesting that secondary synaptic pathology may contribute to spatial organization of microgliosis beyond diffuse myelin loss alone. Prolonged CPZ exposure expanded the high-microgliosis compartment stereotypically, whereas withdrawal produced spatially ordered partial resolution with persistence of a high-microgliosis core and partial visual recovery. Former high-microgliosis territories showed partial restoration of synaptic density despite myelin recovery comparable to persistent high-microgliosis regions. In contrast, female CPZ-treated mice developed widespread SC demyelination and microgliosis without comparable compartmentalization, demonstrating sex-differential organization of microglial reactivity. Together, these findings identify the human SC as a site of demyelinating injury in MS and establish the CPZ-treated mouse SC as a sex-sensitive in vivo framework for investigating spatially patterned microglial reactivity, synaptic pathology, and incomplete resolution of microgliosis after demyelination.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Neuroimmune transcriptional signatures across repeat expansion ataxias in the human brain.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Zhongbo Chen; Amy R Hicks; Jonathan Brenton; Melissa Grant-Peters; Regina H Reynolds; Clarissa Rocca; Guillermo Rocamora-Perez; Raquel Garza
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Hereditary ataxias are neurodegenerative disorders characterised by progressive cerebellar dysfunction, most commonly caused by pathogenic repeat expansions of short tandem DNA repeats. Despite shared genetic mechanisms, the downstream molecular processes leading to neurodegeneration remain incompletely understood. RNA dysregulation has been proposed as a key contributor, but transcriptome-wide changes in human brain tissue across multiple ataxia subtypes have been poorly characterised. This study aims to identify shared and disease-specific transcriptional signatures across repeat expansion ataxias. We used bulk and single nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNAseq) to analyse post-mortem brain tissue from individuals with repeat expansion ataxias in order to gain further mechanistic insight into disease biology. We analysed paired cerebellar and frontal cortex RNA-sequencing data from post-mortem brain tissue obtained from 23 donors with ataxia and 22 age- and sex-matched controls across two brain banks (including spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA)1, SCA2, SCA6, Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA), and cases with unknown molecular diagnoses). Bulk and snRNAseq analyses were used to examine transcript usage, differential gene expression, and cell-type-specific transcriptional changes and biological pathways across disease groups. These analyses revealed extensive transcriptional alterations in ataxia cases, affecting not only the cerebellum but also the frontal cortex. Across genetic subtypes, immune and inflammatory pathways were consistently activated and were associated with transcriptional changes in non-neuronal cell populations, alongside downregulation of neuronal and synaptic processes in the cerebellum. These findings were supported by snRNAseq, which demonstrated that immune-related transcriptional changes were most prominent in non-neuronal cell populations, including microglia and astrocytes. This process was accompanied by neuronal loss and relative expansion of glial populations in the cerebellum. Shared transcriptional signatures were evident across both molecularly diagnosed and undiagnosed cases. Hereditary ataxias are associated with common activation of immune and inflammatory pathways across brain regions and genetic subtypes, with prominent involvement of non-neuronal cell types. These findings highlight immune signalling as a shared feature of disease biology and suggest that inflammatory pathways may represent potential targets for therapeutic intervention. This study provides a comprehensive transcriptomic framework for understanding mechanisms underlying repeat expansion ataxias in the human brain.

top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: A novel α-synuclein (syn) seed amplification assay (synSAA) differentiates 2 types of syn-seeds in CSF: type1, associated with Lewy bodies (LBs), and type2, associated with glial-cytoplasmic inclusions, the hallmark of multiple system atrophy (MSA). However, syn-copathology extends beyond synucleinopathies, and copathologies are increasingly relevant. Different syn-seeds have been assessed in highly characterized research cohorts, but data assessing type and frequency in patients from routine clinical encounters are lacking. Hence, our objective was to determine frequency, type, and clinical association of different syn-seeds in CSF in a large cohort from a movement disorders (MDs) clinic. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included consecutive patients from a MD clinic between 2009 and 2025. CSF was tested with synSAA and clinical data derived from medical records. RESULTS: We recruited 1,059 patients (mean age 70.5 ± 10.5 years; 38.4% female; mean disease duration 4.0 ± 4.6 years). Syn-seeds were detected in 54.2% of patients, with type1-seeds predominating (88.5%). High synSAA positivity was observed in Parkinson disease (PD) (84.7%), dementia with LB (93.4%), MSA (84.5%), isolated REM-sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) (80.0%), and normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) with PD (87.0%). Undetermined hypokinetic MD showed 53.7% positivity. Moderate proportions (∼25-33%) were detected in Alzheimer disease, progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal syndrome, and idiopathic NPH without PD, while other neurologic disorders showed 20.9% positivity. Type2-seeds were the major seed type in MSA (79.6% of syn-seeds) and minor type in PD (6.2%), PSP (9.1%), and undetermined hypokinetic MD (13.8%). Overall, type2-seeds were present in only 2.6% of non-MSA patients. Patients with type1-seeds had worse olfaction and more hallucinations. Multivariable regression identified impaired olfaction (OR = 0.67 per point increase of identified smells out of 12, higher scores indicating better olfaction) significantly associated with type1-seeds. DISCUSSION: Our results provide reference data on syn-seed frequency in routine clinical patients, demonstrating that type1-seeds indicate common underlying syn-pathology or copathology associated with hyposmia and hallucinations. Type2-seeds are specific to MSA and detection of type2-seeds outside the clinical MSA spectrum can improve diagnosis of patients with atypical presentations because our results match neuropathologic MSA studies. In vivo identification of different seed types will improve diagnosis, clinical trial stratification, and development of targeted therapies.

global_hot_topics.title: Mitochondrial protein import stress augments α-synuclein aggregation and neural damage.
global_hot_topics.authors: Liam P Coyne; Arnav Rana; Xiaowen Wang; Joseph Mauro; Sanaea Bhagwagar; Yumiko Umino; Eduardo C Solessio; Frank Middleton
global_hot_topics.abstract: Genetic and environmental factors are known to converge on mitochondria to cause Parkinson's disease. The underlying mechanism is incompletely understood. In addition to bioenergetic defects, nonbioenergetic pathways have been largely unexplored. Validating the nonbioenergetic mitochondrial stressors as independent pathogenic factors is challenging because most mouse models of mitochondrial stress are confounded by bioenergetic defects. Here, we show that expression of Ant1P.A114P,A123D, previously shown to cause mitochondrial protein import clogging in cultured human cells, does not affect the overall bioenergetic capacity, yet it induces proteostatic stress responses in the cytosol that suggests accumulation of unimported precursor proteins. In a Parkinson's disease model expressing α-synuclein (A53T), Ant1P.A114P,A123D increased the size of α-synuclein aggregates, increased aggregation of mitochondrial preproteins, heightened neuroinflammation, and worsened motor coordination defects. Importantly, we found no evidence of bioenergetic defects in either α-synuclein (A53T) or α-synuclein (A53T) + Ant1P.A114P,A123D mice. These data suggest that Ant1P.A114P,A123D likely induces mitochondrial protein import stress, and contributes to neural damage through cytosolic proteostatic stress and altered aggregation dynamics of neuropathogenic proteins independent of bioenergetics.

global_hot_topics.authors: Jean-Philippe Chaput; Yin Wu; Aurélie Baillot; Pavlos K Papasavas; J Graham Thomas; Hollie A Raynor; Dale S Bond
global_hot_topics.abstract: BACKGROUND: While metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) leads to substantial weight loss, objective multidimensional assessments of sleep health in free-living adults after surgery are limited. This study examined associations between weight loss and actigraphy-assessed sleep health indicators among adults undergoing MBS. METHODS: Data were pooled from two prospective cohort studies including 100 adults scheduled for sleeve gastrectomy or Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Participants wore wrist-worn accelerometers for 7-10 days at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months post-surgery. Five sleep health indicators, including sleep regularity, wake-up time variability, sleep duration, sleep efficiency, and sleep timing, were derived using GGIR. Percent total weight loss (%TWL) was calculated at each follow-up. Linear mixed models assessed changes over time and associations between sleep changes and %TWL, adjusting for wear time and relevant covariates. RESULTS: Mean %TWL was 22.1 ± 6.2% at 6 months and 24.8 ± 8.8% at 12 months. No significant group-level changes in sleep indicators were observed (all p ≥ 0.20). However, greater %TWL was associated with better sleep regularity, reflected by higher Sleep Regularity Index scores (B = 0.349, p = 0.02) and lower wake-up time variability (B = -0.044, p = 0.04). Sleep duration, efficiency, and timing were not significantly associated with %TWL. At baseline, sleep duration (8.2 h/day), efficiency (86.8%), and midpoint (2:53 a.m.) were within recommended ranges, whereas Sleep Regularity Index scores were low (33.5), indicating substantial day-to-day variability in sleep timing. CONCLUSIONS: MBS did not improve overall sleep health, but greater postoperative weight loss was linked to better sleep regularity.

global_hot_topics.title: Label-free multi-metric pipeline for reproducible clustering of single-cell RNA-seq cell types.
global_hot_topics.authors: Zachary Yousef; Jonah Simone; Dylan Klein; Avinav Bhuyan; Heejoo Jen Cho; Priya Bhatt; Jiawei Wu; Hongyi Wang
global_hot_topics.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing has transformed our ability to identify cell types and explore cellular diversity. However, determining whether apparent cell subtypes represent true biological populations or artifacts of data analysis remains a major challenge. To address this issue, we developed scClustBench, an open-source benchmarking framework that evaluates cluster quality, stability, and reproducibility across multiple analytical approaches. Rather than relying on a single clustering method, scClustBench tests whether proposed cell subtypes can be consistently recovered. We applied scClustBench to a mouse retinal dataset containing bipolar cells, which are known to exhibit subtype diversity, and rod photoreceptors, for which subtype classification remains controversial. The framework consistently identified reproducible bipolar cell subtypes across analytical methods. In contrast, while some rod photoreceptor clusters appeared stable during resampling analyses, they could not be reproduced across embedding methods, suggesting that these partitions do not represent robust biological subtypes. Additional analyses using simulated and external datasets demonstrated that scClustBench reliably distinguishes meaningful cellular heterogeneity from analytical artifacts. These findings provide a practical framework for rigorous interpretation of single-cell transcriptomic data.

global_hot_topics.title: Semantic Processing in Unresponsive Patients With Acute Brain Injury.
global_hot_topics.authors: Ayham Alkhachroum; Brian Manolovitz; John McKeown; Ana Bolanos; Elena Mishkovsky; Julia Houshmand; Gabriela Aklepi; Mariana Barrios
global_hot_topics.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Early prognostication after acute brain injury (ABI) is challenging because behavioral responsiveness may not accurately reflect preserved cognitive function. Neural responses to semantic incongruity can identify language processing despite the absence of overt behavior. We investigated whether bedside EEG could detect semantic processing in unresponsive patients with ABI and whether its presence was associated with long-term outcomes. METHODS: In this prospective 2-center cohort study, unresponsive adults with ABI admitted to neurologic intensive care units between 2022 and 2025 underwent bedside EEG during a language paradigm comparing congruent and incongruent sentence endings (e.g., "my favorite color is green/soon"). Semantic processing was defined by differential event-related responses within centroparietal channels (300-500 milliseconds) using cluster-based permutation testing with false discovery rate correction. Outcomes were assessed for recovery of consciousness and functional recovery (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score ≥4) at 12 months by blinded interviewers. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, accuracy, and likelihood ratios. RESULTS: Among 105 patients (mean age 58 ± 19 years; 21% women; 53% Hispanic/Latino), the most common etiologies were intracerebral hemorrhage (45%), traumatic brain injury (43%), and subarachnoid hemorrhage (10%). Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy occurred in 31%. Semantic processing was detected in 13 patients (12%). Recovery of consciousness occurred in 77% of patients with semantic processing compared with 49% without semantic processing (odds ratio [OR] 3.5; 95% CI 0.9-13.5, p = 0.08). Functional recovery occurred in 42% with semantic processing compared with 14% without semantic processing (OR 4.5; 95% CI 1.2-16.6, p = 0.03). Semantic processing was highly specific but insensitive for predicting both recovery of consciousness (specificity 94%, sensitivity 18%) and functional recovery (specificity 92%, sensitivity 29%). After excluding patients who underwent withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy or died of non-neurologic medical complications, specificity increased to 100% for recovery of consciousness and 95% for functional recovery. DISCUSSION: EEG evidence of semantic processing can be detected in a subset of unresponsive patients with ABI during the acute phase of injury and is associated with favorable long-term outcomes. Semantic processing was a specific but insensitive biomarker of recovery, suggesting potential utility as a rule-in marker of preserved cognitive function. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multicenter cohorts before clinical implementation.

global_hot_topics.title: Glia and CED-1/MEGF10 independently drive dopamine neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease models.
global_hot_topics.authors: German Rojas; Sneha Ray; Solomon Wossene; Irini Topalidou; Aakanksha Singhvi
global_hot_topics.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is marked by progressive dopamine neuron degeneration, but the phagocytic receptors and cells that clear neuronal corpses remain ill-defined. Moreover, while other cell types like glia, epithelia, and muscle are also impacted in PD, their roles in disease progression are unclear. We report that multiple nonneuronal cell types modulate dopamine neurodegeneration in Caenorhabditis elegans. Astrocyte-like CEPsh glia respond to neuronal stress and regulate dopamine biosynthesis enzyme CAT-2/TH and transporter DAT-1/SLC6A3. They are neurotoxic by downregulating neuroprotective dopamine levels. Degenerating dopamine neurons expose phosphatidylserine (PS) via the necrotic phospholipid scramblase ANOH-1/TMEM16F and ABC transporter CED-7/ABCA1. Epithelia and muscle cells then phagocytose dopamine neuron corpses and drive neuron death and clearance via the conserved PS receptor CED-1/Draper/MEGF10. Depleting ced-1 protects against loss of dopamine neurons and associated animal behaviors in a PD model. Evolutionary conservation of the underlying components and their effects across PD models suggests that multi-organ engagement may be a shared feature of dopamine neurodegeneration in PD.

Moreover, while other cell types like glia, epithelia, and muscle are also impacted in PD, their roles in disease progression are unclear. We report that multiple nonneuronal cell types modulate dopamine neurodegeneration in Caenorhabditis elegans. Astrocyte-like CEPsh glia respond to neuronal stress and regulate dopamine biosynthesis enzyme CAT-2/TH and transporter DAT-1/SLC6A3. They are neurotoxic by downregulating neuroprotective dopamine levels. Degenerating dopamine neurons expose phosphatidylserine (PS) via the necrotic phospholipid scramblase ANOH-1/TMEM16F and ABC transporter CED-7/ABCA1. Depleting ced-1 protects against loss of dopamine neurons and associated animal behaviors in a PD model. Evolutionary conservation of the underlying components and their effects across PD models suggests that multi-organ engagement may be a shared feature of dopamine neurodegeneration in PD.

global_hot_topics.title: Metabolic syndrome and Alzheimer's disease: Mechanistic links and precision prevention (Review).
global_hot_topics.authors: Hanlu Chen; Tao Ding; Yifan Zhu; Mei Yang; Fangsheng Wang; Puwen Chen; Haihong Lin; Huapei Kang
global_hot_topics.abstract: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is associated with increased risk of Alzheimer's disease (AD), however, the majority of previous studies regard MetS as an isolated risk factor and focus on single pathways, lacking systematic understanding of combined effects among multiple metabolic components. The present review systematically summarizes the multifaceted mechanisms by which MetS promotes AD pathology, including insulin resistance and cerebral energy dysregulation, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation and glial cell activation, vascular dysfunction and dysregulation of the renin‑angiotensin system, as well as the central convergent signaling pathway involving glycogen synthase kinase‑3β. The present review further highlights emerging regulatory mechanisms involving the gut‑brain axis, epigenetic reprogramming, sex differences and hormonal effects and senescent microenvironment. By emphasizing the peripheral‑central crosstalk and interactive amplification of MetS components, the present review aimed to position AD as a central manifestation of systemic metabolic disorders in the brain and propose a multi‑domain precision strategy integrating lifestyle intervention, metabolic drug repurposing, gut microbiota regulation, anti‑aging therapy and biomarker‑guided subtype classification for intervention against MetS‑associated AD.

global_hot_topics.title: Pearls & Oy-sters: Anti-GABA
global_hot_topics.authors: Kellie E Krohn; Rebecca Luke; Adrian Lacy; Jonathan D Santoro; John Honeycutt; Sandy Cope-Yokoyama; Alfred Balasa
global_hot_topics.abstract: A previously healthy 5-year-old girl presented with several days of fever/malaise followed by acute neurologic decline. Head CT demonstrated fulminant right cerebellitis with edema and fourth-ventricle effacement concerning for impending herniation. She underwent emergent posterior fossa decompression. CSF showed mild pleocytosis, and MRI revealed right cerebellar nonenhancing T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintense lesions with evolving supratentorial cortical involvement. Despite empiric antimicrobials and initial immunotherapy (high-dose IV methylprednisolone and tocilizumab followed by IV immunoglobulin/plasma exchange), she developed progressive neuroinflammation with new seizures and markedly elevated CSF IL-6, prompting escalation to additional IL-6-directed therapy with tocilizumab and rescue intrathecal dexamethasone. She subsequently stabilized with radiographic improvement and meaningful neurologic recovery. Expanded antibody testing later confirmed anti-GABAA receptor (anti-GABAAR) encephalitis. This case highlights fulminant cerebellitis as a life-threatening presentation of anti-GABAAR encephalitis and underscores the importance of early posterior fossa decompression, parallel diagnostic evaluation (including expanded antibody panels), and coordinated, time-sensitive immunotherapy escalation in select critically ill presentations.

Although studies have linked GLP-1 medications to a lower risk of dementia, major trials found that semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer's disease. Scientists suspect these drugs may be more effective at preserving memory and thinking abilities in people with obesity or diabetes, especially before cognitive problems appear.
